notes.1a: Most candidates obtained results in line with those expected in that as the volume of aqueous sodium thiosulfate decreased the time taken for the text to not be visible increased. The recording of time to the nearest whole number was done my a large number of candidates. It is generally not appropriate to quote reaction times in tenths or hundredths of a second for chemistry experiments due to factors like limitations in measurement precision.
notes.1b: Most of the graphs had a suitable scale on the y-axis, usually 2 cm grid square = 10 seconds. Some candidates selected difficult scales where each 2 cm grid square was 1.5 or 3; these candidates often made errors in plotting. Each large grid square should be 1, 2 or 5  10n. The points were generally correctly plotted. There were many who thought that lines of best fit must be straight lines. The curves of best fit were often poorly drawn. Straight sections on a curve of best fit, very thick lines, wobbly lines or any double line where a gap is visible between the lines is not acceptable.
notes.1c: (i) Candidates performed well on this question and were able to calculate the relative rate using the formula given. Candidates who did not evaluate the fraction gained no credit as there had been no attempt at a calculation.
notes.1cii: This was one of the most accessible questions on the paper and almost all candidates could identify that experiment 1 had the greatest relative rate.
notes.1d: (i) Most candidates were able to calculate the volume of water and give the appropriate unit. Less well performing candidates found this question difficult as they had not understood that the total volume of solution had to remain constant. They often gained credit for units even with an incorrect calculation.
notes.1dii: Nearly all candidates could work out the relevant time for the text to not be visible at 37 cm3. To gain full credit, working had to be shown as stated in the question. The clearest working is the use of construction lines. Candidates who performed less well chose the incorrect volume; the most common was using 36 or 38.5 cm3 rather than 37 cm3.
notes.1iii: Candidates performed poorly on this question and found it very challenging. Most candidates just restated ‘so that the total volume is kept constant’ or said so that ‘it is a fair test’. Few appreciated that if the total volume changes between experiments, you are introducing a second variable, which would make it unclear whether any changes in reaction rate are due to concentration or to volume.
notes.1e: (i) This was the most accessible question on the paper with almost all candidates understanding that burettes measure volumes more accurately than measuring cylinders.
notes.1eii: This question was answered well. Candidates were able to state that either pipettes had fixed volumes or that the pipette sizes available were too small and could not hold the larger variable volumes of sodium thiosulfate required.
notes.1f: This was found to be the most challenging question on the paper and few correct answers were seen. Many candidates incorrectly related their answer to surface area and rate of reaction without realising that a beaker will have a larger cross section and so result in a shallower depth of liquid; this makes it easier to see through and so it takes more time for the text to be obscured.
notes.2a: The expected observations on solution L with aqueous sodium carbonate were a white precipitate forming and effervescence. Many candidates noted one out of these two. Better performing candidates were guided by the mark allocation of [2] and realised that two observations were expected.
notes.2b: As the question stated that NaOH should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is formed on dropwise addition which should dissolve in excess. Some candidates gave answers which suggested they did not mix the contents of the boiling tube when adding in excess and so reported a white precipitate at the bottom and a colourless solution above. A few candidates reported precipitates that were not white, but this is impossible due to solution L containing the aluminium salt.
notes.2c: Similarly, as the question stated that aqueous ammonia should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is formed on dropwise addition which should remain excess. Some candidates gave answers which suggested they did not mix the contents of the boiling tube when adding in excess and so reported a white precipitate at the bottom and a colourless solution above – that colourless solution would be aqueous ammonia that has not mixed with the precipitate. Several candidates mixed up the observations for (b) and (c) and care should be taken to note the observations in the correct answer spaces.
notes.2d: Most candidates reported the expected white precipitate. It was not uncommon for candidates to report a cream precipitate. Candidates should be familiar with the colours of silver halide precipitates, comparing the precipitate colour to a sheet of white paper can help determine if the precipitate is white or cream. Some candidates reported that there was no change – the most probable reason for this is adding incorrect reagents when they performed the test.
notes.2e: Those candidates who obtained correct observations were generally successful in identifying the salt as aluminium and chloride. Candidates often stated the ions in solid L and this gained full credit, but it should be noted that the term ‘chlorine ion’ is not accepted for ‘chloride ion’.
notes.2f: The expected flame test colour was green for solid M. Candidates received credit if they gave the expected colour or a colour that matched the supervisor’s results. If the supervisor results for Question 2 are not submitted, then the only accepted answer is the expected colour of green; it is essential that supervisor results are submitted for Questions 1 and 2.
notes.2g: (i) The test carried out was the test for nitrate ions and the expected result was effervescence and red litmus turning blue. Many candidates gained credit for stating that the gas produced turned red litmus blue but did not state that effervescence was seen. ‘Gas produced’ is not an observation but a conclusion from the effervescence seen.
notes.2gii: Most candidates noted the formation of a white precipitate as solid M was a barium salt.
notes.2h: Candidates who performed well often gained full credit for the identification of solid M as barium nitrate. It was not uncommon for candidates to identify only that solid M contained barium ions and not include an anion in their answer.
notes.3: This planning question was well answered with many candidates gaining full credit. Candidates made good use of the information provided. This was a task which involved the preparation of a pure, dry sample of solid lead(II) chloride. Most candidates used a method based on the information in the question. The expected steps in the plan were: • addition of water to solid lead(II) nitrate and addition of water to solid sodium chloride • stirring the mixtures so that both solids dissolved forming aqueous solutions • addition of both the aqueous solutions together • using a suitable container such as a beaker or boiling tube • filtration of the precipitate from the aqueous sodium nitrate • washing of the precipitate with water to remove aqueous sodium nitrate impurities • drying of the precipitate by leaving in a warm place. Many excellent and succinct answers were seen. However, a common reason for candidates not obtaining full credit was the omission of details. For example, some candidates did not specify stirring to aid dissolving or washing and drying the precipitate. Candidates who performed less well did not dissolve the solids at the start and began their method by adding the aqueous solutions together. A small number of candidates added the solids together so the precipitation reaction would not work. A significant minority confused the terms filtrate and residue. Some candidates choose unsuitable pieces of equipment for making their salt such as a burette, measuring cylinder, volumetric flask or trough. Suitable containers would include beakers, conical flasks, boiling tubes or test-tubes. A small number of candidates gained no credit for drying the precipitate as no method of drying was given. ‘Dry’ is not sufficient but ‘leave to dry in a warm place’ would gain credit. There is no need for candidates to write a list of aims and apparatus at the start of their answers. The aim of the plan is in the question and credit will not be given for listing items of apparatus; where credit is available for the selection of an appropriate item of apparatus then it must be clear in the plan for what the item of apparatus will be used. Writing a list of dependent, independent and control variables is also not necessary.
notes.general_comments:
The vast majority of candidates successfully attempted all the questions and the full range of marks was
seen. Most candidates were able to complete the questions in the time available. The paper discriminated
successfully between candidates of different abilities but was accessible to all and was generally well-
answered, with very few blank spaces.
